decisions.quote: Across participants and sessions, mean appropriate engagement increased from 5% in baseline to 27% with intervention, compared with increases from 41% to 81% in Engelman et al. (1999) and 39% to 85% in LeBlanc et al. (2006). Despite higher absolute levels of engagement with check-in reported in previous studies, the relative increase from base- line to check-in of 440% in our study still may be socially significant.
decisions.reason: Testing the check-in procedure of Engelman, Altus, and Mathews (1999; doi: 10.1901/jaba.1999.32-107) in a new sample of five nursing home residents with severe dementia (replication), the outcome is successful. Addressing the parent scope objection: the prior review erred by inferring a mixed outcome from participant responder counts (three clear responders, one modest responder, and one nonresponder vs. five of five in Engelman et al., 1999). The authors never contrast their responder count against Engelman et al. as a failed or partial replication. Instead, when directly comparing their results to Engelman et al. (1999), the authors aggregate across participants and sessions, showing that mean appropriate engagement increased in the same direction (from 5% at baseline to 27% during check-in, a 440% relative increase that they interpret as potentially socially significant) and that mean inappropriate engagement decreased (from 5% to 1%, vs. <1% to 0% in Engelman et al.). Their 'In contrast' sentence regarding inappropriate engagement and discussion of MMSE scores (0-3 vs. 4-19 in Engelman et al.) explain why absolute baseline and intervention levels differed in a more severely impaired extension sample, not a contradicted treatment effect, and noting that check-in 'may be beneficial for some participants with advanced dementia' reflects individual heterogeneity in severe dementia rather than a mixed replication verdict. Under the codebook, smaller absolute effects and coder-tallied responder counts without an author-stated contrast do not make a replication mixed.

decisions.quote: We report findings of a replication, with some additional components, to increase appropriate activity engagement among 5 residents (aged 77 to 83 years) with severe dementia. Evaluated in a concurrent multiple baseline design across participants that incorporated partial withdrawal phases, activity engagement increased for 3 participants, with modest improvement for 1 other participant. The 4 responders all engaged in a wider variety of activities during intervention.
decisions.reason: The original study (Engelman et al., 1999) reported that the check-in procedure increased appropriate activity engagement for all five participating residents. Evaluating the procedure in a single-case concurrent multiple baseline design across five participants, the authors explicitly frame their findings as mixed across participants: three participants showed clear increases, one showed modest improvement, and one (Heather) showed no change during the intervention, leading the authors to conclude that the procedure 'may be beneficial for some participants with advanced dementia' while nonresponders require a more intensive individualized approach.

scope_review.parent_objection: The first review retains mixed by comparing five original responders with three clear responders plus one modest responder in the new single-case series. Codebook forbids own count-based mixed judgments and says differences in effect size alone are not mixed when the substantive claim is retained. Source directly compares mean appropriate engagement increases and says the relative440%increase may still be sociallysignificant; inappropriate engagement decreases in both, despite different absolutelevels. Is there an author-stated failed/contradictory original finding, or an overall partial-replication verdict, rather than the reviewer inferring one from participant counts? Read the full text and settle overall outcome under the precise codebook. Do not assume either priorreview or thisobjection right.
